item.title: Vulcan's Hammer by Philip K. Dick
item.description:
A centralized computer runs humanity after a decimating global war.

With this premise, Dick interrogates the effectiveness of withholding information from analysis. Direct information, such as assassinations or riots, should be correlated with economic and social aggregations of data. If the correlations are known beforehand, then the withholding of data leads to a questioning of the reliability of the datasource rather than the proper masking of the sensitive data.

item.title: Kokun: The Girl From the West by Nahoko Uehashi
item.description: Uehashi provides an analysis of empire and agriculture in this fantasy land, asking questions which are similar to those posed by James Scott in Against the Grain. The questions of the state and their role in agrarian systems and enforcing specific agrarian systems above others.

item.title: Dead Souls By Nikolai Gogol
item.description: The title says it all… Well along with the context that Gogol is critiquing the serfdom of the Russian Empire and the legal and financial structures that lead to the emancipation of the surfs. If you want to know more about this, just read the book, it’s a political satire, so it is fun and lighthearted.

item.title: Against the Grain by James Scott
item.description: James Scott gives a foray into a somewhat speculative agriculture of pre-history of Europe and West Asia. The driving premise is that the ‘pre-historical’ agriculture was fairly ecologically stable and widely practiced at the same time as historical agricultural systems. Because the institutions of cities and early states allowed for maintenance of records, our knowledge of historical agricultural systems is biased to preserving agricultural methods which supported cities and states.
